record.paper_title: Modeling social resilience: Questions, answers, open problems
record.original_question: How can one define and measure macro-variables for social organizations that quantify adaptive capacity, elasticity, robustness, and capacity to recover, so that resilience can be monitored over time and early-warning tools can be applied rather than relying only on resources, well-being surveys, or hindsight cases?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a social organization modeled as a time-evolving system whose microscopic state is described by a high-dimensional configuration x(t) ∈ X (e.g., individuals' attributes, interactions, beliefs, or resources) governed by stochastic dynamics, and which is occasionally subject to exogenous perturbations or shocks. Define resilience as a property comprising four distinct facets: (i) adaptive capacity (the ability of the system to reorganize and modify its internal structure in response to changing conditions), (ii) elasticity (the speed and extent to which the system returns toward a reference state after a perturbation), (iii) robustness (the magnitude of perturbations that can be absorbed without qualitative change of state), and (iv) capacity to recover (the long-run probability and rate of return to a viable regime after a major disruption).

Construct a set of macro-variables M₁(t),…,M_k(t), each a functional M_i: X → ℝ of the microscopic state (or of its statistical distribution), together with a precise mathematical definition, such that:

1. Each macro-variable quantifies one of the four facets above, in a way that is operationally measurable from time-series observations of the system.
2. The macro-variables can be monitored continuously over time, so that statistical signatures (such as critical slowing down, variance inflation, or autocorrelation changes) can serve as early-warning indicators of loss of resilience before a regime shift occurs.
3. The definitions do not reduce resilience to the mere availability of resources, to subjective well-being survey responses, or to ex-post identification from historical case studies of collapse or survival.
4. The proposed macro-variables admit a rigorous derivation from an underlying agent-based or stochastic dynamical model of the social organization, and their behavior under generic perturbations can be analyzed mathematically.

Provide such a definition together with a proof or justification that the chosen macro-variables capture the four facets of resilience and support early-warning detection.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of defining quantitative macro-variables for social resilience that capture adaptive capacity, elasticity, robustness, and recovery is widely acknowledged as open in the literature on social systems modeling and complex-systems resilience theory. Existing approaches (e.g., critical-slowing-down indicators in ecology, network robustness metrics) provide partial tools, but no consensus operational definition for social organizations exists.

status_evidence.title: Modeling social resilience: Questions, answers, open problems
status_evidence.snippet: The work explicitly notes that social systems lack macro-variables for resilience and lists this as an open problem.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is posed as an open modeling challenge.
